chunks: And from him, from Isma'il ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, who said:

I asked him about a man who marries temporarily (mut'ah) from the Jews and the Christians. He said, 'I see no harm in that.' I said, 'And from the Magians?' He said, 'As for the Magians, then no (not permissible).'

His saying, peace be upon him, 'As for the Magians, then no,' indicates the place of dislike (karahah). And when one is able to marry from others (Jews/Christians), but in the state of necessity, there is no harm in it. He narrated that.

key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةِ: Dislike (a level of impermissibility or preference against)

ai.seo_question: Is temporary marriage with Zoroastrians permissible in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling to clarify the distinction between the People of the Book (Jews and Christians), with whom temporary marriage is permissible, and the Magians (Zoroastrians), where it is disliked (karahat) but valid. The scholar notes that while the Magian ruling carries a tone of dislike, it remains permissible in cases of necessity (idtirar), reflecting the broader Shia jurisprudential principle of treating Magians as a distinct category of monotheists. This hadith is crucial for understanding the flexibility of mut'ah across different religious communities in early Islamic society.
